newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy distances itself from Albania's Berisha.
newsitem.headline: Italy distances itself from Albania's Berisha.

text.p: Italy signalled on Saturday that it no longer saw Albanian President Sali Berisha as a key player in his crisis-hit country's affairs and said his fate was in the hands of the Balkan state's new premier.
"It's up to Prime Minister (Bashkim) Fino to assess what Berisha's role might now be," Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told the newspaper La Repubblica.
He said Fino had to decide whether Berisha's presence was "an obstacle to pacifying the country or not, whether his continuation in the role can be accepted at least to prepare elections or not".
The comments marked a clear distancing from Berisha by Italy, Albania's biggest economic partner and a leading force in diplomatic efforts to halt the country's descent into chaos.

Rome had been regarded as the right-wing president's closest contact in the European Union until armed rebellion and anarchy spread through the impoverished state this month. He sent his son and daughter to safety in Italy on Thursday.
In the Dutch town of Apeldoorn, where EU foreign ministers were discussing the crisis, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said openly that Berisha should resign.

"I'm sure that if President Berisha were to step down that would in some ways improve the situation in Albania," said Petersen, whose country holds the chairmanship of the 54-member Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

Dini noted that leaders from rebel towns in Albania's south had told OSCE mediator Franz Vranitzky during talks on an Italian warship on Friday that while they supported Fino's national unity government they wanted Berisha to go.
"The (rebel) committees said that they will hand in their weapons only after Berisha has resigned," he said.
Berisha, whose Democratic Party won a landslide in elections last year which international observers said were deeply flawed, has given no indication that he intends to quit.
His re-election to a second five-year term by parliament went ahead on March 3 as armed unrest sparked by the collapse of shady pyramid savings schemes engulfed the south.
He initially refused to form a new coalition government in response to the uprising but bowed to international pressure last weekend by agreeing to a deal with opposition parties.
Fino, of the main opposition Socialists, heads a government of national reconciliation which is meant to lead the country to internationally supervised early elections by June.
Italy had pressed hard for an all-party government to be set up. "Fino is now our primary interlocutor," one diplomat said.
Dini defended past contacts with Berisha, saying he was "and for the moment remains the constituted authority" in Albania.
But he was critical of Berisha's late agreement to a unity government.
"My great regret is that the formation of the new government happened so late," Dini said. "The dramatic developments of these past few days could have been avoided."
